dimension: Peer-to-peer coordination with no central server, and reputation among untrusted peers
citations_that_failed: None fabricated. All 10 cited works exist, are correctly attributed, and the verbatim quotes are real and correctly located. Specifics verified: Cohen, 'Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent', P2PECON 2003 (fetched bittorrent.org/bittorrentecon.pdf). Legout/Urvoy-Keller/Michiardi, IMC 2006 - CrossRef 10.1145/1177080.1177106 returns title, 3 authors, pp. 203-216, ACM 2006, exactly as cited; arXiv cs/0609026 is the same paper. Legout/Liogkas/Kohler/Zhang, arXiv cs/0611105 - abstract contains 'instrumented private torrent', 'decisions of more than 40 nodes', and 'an underprovisioned initial seed leads to the absence of peer clustering and less effective sharing incentives', all as cited. Piatek et al., NSDI 2007 - all 4 numbers confirmed in the text: 'median 70% performance gain', 'CDF of download performance for 114 real' swarms, 'factor of 1.72 with 25% of downloads finishing at least twice as fast', 'average completion time for a low capacity peer moves from 314 to 733 seconds'. Levin/LaCurts/Spring/Bhattacharjee, SIGCOMM 2008 - CrossRef 10.1145/1402958.1402987 returns pp. 243-254 exactly; abstract line verified: 'we prove that a proportional-share client is strategy-proof'. Douceur, IPTPS 2002 - CrossRef 10.1007/3-540-45748-8_24 returns pp. 251-260; Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 quotes are verbatim. Andrade/Brasileiro/Cirne/Mowbray, HPDC 2004 - the sqrt formula IS real and IS Subsection 3.1 equation (4), verbatim: 'rA(B) = max{0, v(B,A) - v(A,B) + sqrt(v(B,A))}'. Friedman and Resnick - 'Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, 10(2):173-199, June 2001', confirmed against the PropShare reference list. RFC 9162 Section 1 - all 3 quoted fragments verbatim. draft-ietf-trans-gossip-05 - rev 05, 2018-01-14, IESG state 'Expired (Dead)', never an RFC, consistent with 'expired July 2018'.
quantitative_errors: Cohen 2003 Section 3.2 measures rate as 'a rolling 20-second average'; the 10 seconds is the RECHOKE PERIOD ('BitTorrent peers recalculate who they want to choke once every ten seconds'). The dimension says the rank is by 'the data rate it has measured FROM them over the last 10 seconds', conflating the window with the period. The averaging window is 20 s.

'unchokes 1 additional interested peer chosen uniformly at random' - Cohen never states uniformity, and Cohen Section 3.4 (anti-snubbing) explicitly breaks the stated bound: 'This frequently results in more than one concurrent optimistic unchoke, (an exception to the exactly one optimistic unchoke rule mentioned above)'. So 'exploration budget is bounded at roughly 1 of 4 slots' is not an invariant of the deployed algorithm; under snubbing it is exceeded. If CDSFL copies the budget as a hard cap it is copying something BitTorrent does not actually hold to.

Douceur Lemma 1 is 'f can present g = floor(rho) distinct identities'. The dimension drops the floor and writes 'g = rho'. At rho just under 2 the real bound is 1 identity, not 2 - the floor is what makes the bound weak at small resource ratios, which is exactly the regime a 1-to-700 roster of small seats sits in.

'Three of his four lemmas apply to it directly' is unsupported. Lemma 3 and Lemma 4 are both inside Section 3.2 INDIRECT identity validation and are conditioned on 'if local entity l accepts any identity vouched for by q accepted identities'. A startup maths problem with no vouching triggers Lemmas 1 and 2 only - which is all the dimension's own argument actually invokes, plus the Section 3.2 puzzle-combining passage, which is not a lemma. Correct count is 2 of 4.

OurGrid: equation (4) is cited correctly but is NOT the form the paper carries evidence for. Subsection 3.2 states: 'The results for the two reputation functions with history terms (Equations 3 and 4) were very similar, so we will not report those for the function given in Equation 4.' The reported history-term function is equation (3), the log form. The dimension presents eq. 4 as 'an explicit formula' that solves the constraint; it is one of two offered examples ('we use a sublinear function ... for example'), and the unreported one.
overstated_verdicts: INVERTED READING, and it is the load-bearing one. The dimension says 'Douceur's section 3.2 closes the obvious patch' and concludes 'even enforcing simultaneity does not save a maths-problem challenge: a single endpoint can answer all m concurrent challenges as m apparent participants.' Douceur does the opposite. Immediately after the combining construction he writes: 'An obvious danger here is that if a validating entity issues challenges to multiple identities that have been counterfeited by a single faulty entity, the faulty entity could combine the challenges and solve them together. However, the challenger can identify this attempted Sybil attack by checking whether x1|y1|z1 = x2|y2|z2 for any two solutions from putatively different identities.' The acknowledgements thank Dan Simon 'for sanity checking the combinable computational puzzle described in Section 3.2'. The source supplies a constant-time detection test for precisely the attack the dimension says is undefeatable. The disagreement survives in weakened form - Lemma 2 does bite a recursive, round-structured startup ladder, and Douceur does say 'Lemma 2 is insurmountable for intrinsically temporal resources, such as computation speed' - but the claim that this is 'a formal result, not a judgement' is not supported for the batching leg, which is the leg the dimension uses to close off the simultaneity fix.

PropShare DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE, cold-start cell: 'A contributor with a tiny contribution gets a proportionally tiny but NON-ZERO share, so there is no discrete threshold to clear. This removes the need for a separate newcomer-exception mechanism.' Directly contradicted by the cited paper. Section 5 of Levin et al.: 'Clearly, the prop-share auction requires bootstrapping; peers must give some initial amount of goods to one another to obtain any in return.' Section 9 is titled BOOTSTRAPPING FILE SHARING and gives Algorithm 5, a 3-party protocol (A, existing partner B, newcomer n) with encrypted-block proxy forwarding, concluding: 'The newcomer, n, pays his dues in two ways'. Proportional share of a zero contribution is zero, so a fresh seat gets nothing until bootstrapped. The paper not only keeps a newcomer exception, it makes it a DUES-PAYING one and cites Friedman and Resnick while doing so - which is the same mechanism the dimension's own strongest-disagreement section says collides with the founder's 'never permanently set aside' constraint. The writeup cites PropShare as escaping the dues problem and Friedman-Resnick as proving the dues problem is inescapable, from the same page of the same paper.

BitTorrent choking DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE on the no-coordinator constraint: 'No global state, no coordinator, no identity, no reputation record.' True of the choke algorithm, false of the system as cited. Legout IMC 2006 Section 2: the peer set 'typically consists of 50 peers chosen at random in the list of peers currently involved in the torrent' supplied by the tracker, and 'Each peer reports its state to the tracker every 30 minutes'. Cohen 2003 assumes a tracker and an initial seed throughout. The dimension's strongest-disagreement section attacks CDSFL for needing a coordinator while presenting the 2003 BitTorrent design, which has one for peer discovery, as the coordinator-free alternative. Consequence for roster 700: each seat's 'top 3' is top-of-a-50-sample, not top-of-roster, so even the local ranking is sample-dependent.

Capacity clustering DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE, and 'This IS the answer to ... a little desktop PC against a vast supercomputer stack'. The evidence is 41 PlanetLab nodes in 3 bandwidth classes on a PRIVATE torrent with a single initial seed. That does not reach a 1-to-700 roster, and the paper's own remedy for the failure mode the dimension correctly flags is coordinator-side: its abstract offers 'guidelines for seed provisioning by content providers' and 'a tracker protocol extension that addresses an identified limitation of the protocol'. The fix for the underprovisioned-seed collapse re-adds the coordinator.

'No P2P reputation system in this literature measures capability by having the peer produce its own checkable certificate of competence. That is the one piece worth keeping.' Too strong as written. Solve-expensive / verify-cheap with a challengeable certificate is the whole architecture of Teutsch and Reitwiessner's verification game (Truebit, arXiv 1908.04756, dated 16 Nov 2017), where a Solver returns a result and any Verifier can challenge it, with dispute resolution by bisection. The narrow version of the claim - that no paper in the BitTorrent/OurGrid reciprocity line does this - is defensible; the universal over 'this literature' is not. Better anchor for the novelty claim, from the dimension's own source: the OurGrid authors name their one unsolved issue in the conclusion as 'sabotage tolerance, which is in fact an issue for any resource sharing system'. CDSFL's checkable falsification task is a candidate answer to the exact gap the Network of Favours authors flagged, and that is a stronger and better-evidenced framing of the novelty than a literature-wide negative.

'Floored at 0 so a bad performer cannot be worse off than a newcomer (that is the "never set aside" property)'. The floor gives equality with a newcomer, and in NoF a newcomer's standing is the worst standing there is: 'whenever there is resource contention, requesters with higher reputation get priority', and reputation is 'zero for newcomers'. So a persistently bad performer is served only out of slack capacity, every time any positive-reputation peer competes. That is 'never formally excluded', not 'never set aside'. Under heavy contention with 700 seats the two are operationally different, and the founder's constraint is about the latter.

'the auditability goal and the no-coordinator goal are in direct tension ... should not expect to solve, as a side project, the problem that the global certificate ecosystem has left open for over a decade.' The RFC 9162 quotes are exact and the gossip-draft history is right, but the inference conflates an unsolved DEPLOYMENT problem at global-CA scale and incentives with an unsolved MECHANISM problem. See missed mechanism: timeline entanglement, 2002, with a measured implementation sized at a few hundred mutually distrusting services - which is the regime a 700-seat roster is in.

missed_mechanisms.name: PropShare's own Sybil-proofness proof
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: This is inside a paper the dimension already cites and read, and it defuses the dimension's headline disagreement. Levin et al. Section 6.2 proves prop-share is Sybil-proof: 'To show that prop-share is Sybil-proof, it suffices to show that, for a fixed amount of contribution C, p will receive the same amount of bandwidth for any set of Sybils, including the set of size 1', with equation (2) giving sum over i of Bv*ci/(sum_j cj + yv) = Bv*C/(C + yv), followed by 'In practice, Sybils perform even worse against a prop-share client.' The implication is the direct answer to the Douceur Lemma 1 argument: under PROPORTIONAL allocation, splitting a fixed resource across floor(rho) identities returns exactly what one identity returns, so identity multiplicity buys nothing and the large-rho heterogeneity constraint stops being an attack surface. The dimension argues at length that 'capability is measured, not named' plus 'heterogeneous participants' jointly MAXIMISE the Sybil surface, while recommending as its best transfer the one allocation rule whose authors prove the opposite under their model. That is the single most consequential gap in the writeup.
missed_mechanisms.citation: Dave Levin, Katrina LaCurts, Neil Spring, Bobby Bhattacharjee, 'BitTorrent is an Auction: Analyzing and Improving BitTorrent's Incentives', ACM SIGCOMM 2008, pp. 243-254, DOI 10.1145/1402958.1402987, Section 6.2 and eq. (2).

missed_mechanisms.name: EigenTrust: a global reputation vector computed with no central server
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: The dimension asserts that adopting local reciprocal ranking means 'there is no global ranking any more. "Top tier" stops existing as an object; each requester has its own top 3. If CDSFL needs a single auditable statement of record such as "seat X is tier 1", this mechanism cannot produce one without re-adding an aggregator.' EigenTrust is a direct counterexample: normalised local trust values are aggregated into a global trust vector by distributed left-principal-eigenvector power iteration, each peer computing its own component from its neighbours, with no central aggregator, and with pre-trusted peers supplying the cold-start prior and defending against malicious collectives. Whether its assumptions fit CDSFL is arguable - pre-trusted peers are a named-trust anchor and sit uneasily with 'no routing by model name' - but the impossibility the dimension states is false as stated, and the honest version is a trade-off (distributed iteration cost and a pre-trust set) rather than a wall. Noting also that the OurGrid authors made the opposite choice deliberately: 'in OurGrid we circumvent the need to provide such guarantees by not aggregating a global reputation value for a peer ... there is no attempt to create a global assessment' - so the two cited systems bracket the design space and the dimension reports only one side.
missed_mechanisms.citation: Sepandar D. Kamvar, Mario T. Schlosser, Hector Garcia-Molina, 'The EigenTrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Networks', WWW 2003, p. 640, DOI 10.1145/775152.775242.

missed_mechanisms.name: SybilLimit: a formal Sybil bound with no trusted central authority and no resource challenge
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: The dimension treats Douceur 2002 as the terminal result on identity in a trustless setting, and its whole 'what will fail' conclusion rests on that. The social-network line answers Douceur without resource challenges at all, and does so with a bound: SybilLimit accepts O(log n) sybil nodes per attack edge, improving SybilGuard's O(sqrt(n log n)) per attack edge by Theta(sqrt(n)) - 'around 200 times in our experiments for a million-node system' - and is proved 'at most a log n factor away from optimal, when considering approaches based on fast-mixing social networks'. The abstract frames the exact setting the dimension is in: 'Without a trusted central authority, defending against sybil attacks is quite challenging.' Also relevant to the dimension's startup-tournament critique: the paper notes 'simply monitoring each node's historical behavior is often insufficient because sybil nodes can behave nicely initially, and then launch an attack' - a falsifier of the continuous-measurement mechanism the dimension prefers, not just of the one-shot tournament it attacks. Boundary condition the dimension would be right to raise: SybilLimit needs a social/trust graph among honest participants with few attack edges, and whether a roster of model seats has any such graph is an open question. But the bound exists and must be engaged rather than skipped.
missed_mechanisms.citation: Haifeng Yu, Phillip B. Gibbons, Michael Kaminsky, Feng Xiao, 'SybilLimit: A Near-Optimal Social Network Defense against Sybil Attacks', IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2008, pp. 3-17 (abstract and Table 1).

missed_mechanisms.name: Timeline entanglement: mutually auditable append-only logs among mutually distrusting services
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: This is the specific answer to the registry leg the dimension declares a decade-open problem. RFC 9162's admission is about one log per client view; timeline entanglement removes the single trusted log by binding each service's secure timeline into others', so that a point in one timeline's past is provably bound to a later point in another's, and no single log can show inconsistent views without the entangled peers' records contradicting it. It is not a proposal only: the paper reports Timeweave, built on two disk-based authenticated data structures, supporting a few hundred entangled services at roughly 2 to 8 percent of a PC-grade server's resources. A roster capped at 700 is within an order of magnitude of that measured envelope. So the founder's auditability goal and no-coordinator goal are in TENSION on cost and protocol complexity, not in the direct conflict the dimension asserts, and the right advice is 'budget for entanglement or gossip', not 'do not attempt it'.
missed_mechanisms.citation: Petros Maniatis, Mary Baker, 'Secure History Preservation Through Timeline Entanglement', 11th USENIX Security Symposium, 2002, pp. 297-312 (also arXiv cs/0202005).

Why SOUND_WITH_CORRECTIONS and not UNSOUND: nothing is fabricated. That is unusual and worth stating plainly - 10 of 10 cited works exist, the authors and venues are right, the page ranges that were given are right to the page, and the 3 most load-bearing verbatim quotes (Douceur Lemma 1 and Lemma 2, the OurGrid sqrt equation, the RFC 9162 trusted-third-party sentence) are all real and correctly located. The sqrt term in particular reads like an invented flourish and is not: it is Subsection 3.1 equation (4). The Piatek numbers are 4 for 4.

Why corrections are nevertheless required: one source is read backwards at the point where the argument turns (Douceur Section 3.2 supplies a detection test for puzzle-combining; the dimension says the hole cannot be patched), one DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE cold-start claim is contradicted by its own paper's Section 9, and the dimension's strongest argument is undercut by a Sybil-proofness proof sitting in a paper it cites.

What survives adversarial review intact, and should be told to the founder as surviving: (1) Lemma 2 does break a RECURSIVE, round-structured startup ladder specifically - 'the resources required for each presentation are used and then freed for the subsequent presentation' - and Douceur's own remark that 'Lemma 2 is insurmountable for intrinsically temporal resources, such as computation speed' means no amount of puzzle design fixes a non-simultaneous tournament. That part of the disagreement is correct and above threshold. (2) A knockout bracket does require someone to hold the bracket, and that is a coordinator. Correct. (3) Continuous bounded exploration dominates a one-shot startup rank on staleness grounds. Correct, and Cohen's own stated rationale agrees: long-term transfer totals 'performed poorly because the value of bandwidth shifts rapidly over time'. (4) The underprovisioned-seed caveat on clustering is real, correctly quoted, and is the right warning for CDSFL: if hard well-posed falsification targets are scarce relative to roster size, expect tiering to degenerate. (5) The Friedman-Resnick tension with 'never permanently set aside' is real and is not dissolved by the NoF floor, only softened.

One correction that strengthens rather than weakens the dimension: its novelty claim is better anchored in the OurGrid conclusion, which names 'sabotage tolerance' as the single unsolved implementation issue for autonomous reputation schemes. CDSFL's checkable-falsification probe is a candidate answer to that named gap. That is a defensible, sourced novelty claim; 'no P2P reputation system in this literature' is a universal the dimension did not survey, and Truebit's verification game is a counterexample to the broad reading.
